# Project Overview

This project analyzes employee productivity, salary distribution, and project workload using **R** and **ggplot2**.  
The analysis includes data transformation, summary statistics, and visualization to uncover patterns in employee performance across departments.

## Environment Setup

This analysis uses the following R packages:

- **dplyr** for data manipulation
- **tidyr** for data reshaping
- **ggplot2** for data visualization
- **knitr** for table formatting
- **ggrepel** for text labels readability 
  
```{r loading_packages, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)
library(ggrepel)   
```

### Creating dataset

```{r creating data_frame, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
employee_data <- data.frame(
  employee = c("John", "Mary", "David", "Sarah", "Daniel", 
               "Grace", "Michael", "Linda", "James", "Sophia"),
  department = c("IT", "HR", "IT", "Finance", "IT", 
                 "HR", "Finance", "IT", "HR", "Finance"),
  experience = c(3, 5, 2, 6, 4, 
                 7, 3, 5, 4, 6),
  salary = c(4500, 5200, 4000, 6000, 4800, 
             6500, 4700, 5300, 5000, 6200),
  project = c(5, 6, 3, 7, 4, 
              8, 5, 6, 5, 7),
  hoursworked = c(160, 170, 150, 180, 165, 
                  175, 160, 172, 168, 178)
    )

kable(head(employee_data, 10), 
      caption = "Sample of Employee Data",
      col.names = c("Employee", "Department", "Experience", "Salary", "Project", "HoursWorked"))
```

### Transformation of Data

```{r transformation_of_data}
employee_data_clean <- employee_data %>%
  mutate(salary_per_project = salary / project,
         productivity = project / hoursworked,
         performance = ifelse(project >= 7, "Excellent",
                              ifelse(project >= 5 & project <= 6, "Good",
                                     "Average")))


kable(employee_data_clean %>%
        select(employee, department, salary_per_project, productivity, performance),
      caption = "Transformed Employee Data",
      col.names = c("Employee", "Department", "Salary/Project", "Productivity", "Performance"))
```

### Summary Analysis

The following analysis calculates department-level statistics including average salary, maximum salary, employee count, and productivity.

```{r data_analysis}
summary <- employee_data_clean %>%
  group_by(department) %>%
  summarise(
    avg_salary = mean(salary),
    max_salary = max(salary),
    min_salary = min(salary),
    total_project = sum(project),
    employeecount = n(),
    avg_productivity = mean(productivity)
  )

kable(summary, 
      caption = "Department Summary Statistics",
      col.names = c("Department", "Avg Salary", "Max Salary", 
                    "Min Salary", "Total Projects", "Headcount", "Avg Productivity"),
      digits = 4)

```


## Visualisation

### Average Salary by Department

```{r salary_bar_chart}
ggplot(data = summary, aes(x = reorder(department, avg_salary),
                             y = avg_salary, fill = department)) +
   geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_salary, 1)), vjust = -0.5, size = 4) +
    scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
    labs(
      title = "Average Salary By Department",
      x = "Department",
      y = "Salary"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
    )
```


### Project Per Employee

```{r project_bar_chart}
 ggplot(data = employee_data_clean, aes(x = reorder(employee, project), 
                                          y = project)) +
     geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
     geom_text(aes(label = project), vjust = -0.5) +
     labs(
       title = "Number of Project Per Employee",
       x = "Employee",
       y = "Project"
     ) +
     theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
   
```


### Salary vs Experience

```{r salary_vs_experience}
  ggplot(data = employee_data_clean,
          mapping = aes(x = experience,
                        y = salary, color = department)) +
     geom_point(size = 3) +
     geom_text_repel(aes(label = employee)) +
     scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
     labs(
       title = "Salary vs Experience",
       x = "Years of Experience",
       y = "Monthly Salary"
     ) +
     theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Project vs WorkHours

```{r project_vs_workhours}
 ggplot(data = employee_data_clean, mapping = aes(x = hoursworked, y = project, color = department)) +
     geom_point(size = 3) +
     geom_text_repel(aes(label = employee)) +
     scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
     labs(
       title = "Project vs Hours Worked",
       x = "Number of Hours Worked",
       y = "Project"
     ) +
     theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```


### Salary Distribution

```{r salary_distribution_across_department}
 ggplot(data = employee_data_clean, aes(x = department,
                                    y = salary, fill = department)) +
     geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE) +
     labs(
       title = "Salary Distribution by Department",
       x = "Department",
       y = "Salary"
     ) +
     theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

### Employee Performance Distribution

```{r employee_performance}
ggplot(employee_data_clean, aes(x = performance, fill = performance)) +
     geom_bar(show.legend = FALSE) +
     geom_text(stat = "count", aes(label =  after_stat(count)), vjust = -0.5) +
     scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
     labs(
       title = "Employee Performance Distribution", 
       x = "Rating", 
       y = "Count") +
     theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```



## Summary & Recommendations

### Key Findings

**1. Experience drives salary (+47% gap)**  
Employees with 6–7 years of experience earn an average of $6,233 compared to $4,250 
for those with 2–3 years. Retaining experienced employees yields a significant return.

**2. Finance leads in compensation (22% above IT)**  
Finance averages $6,133 per employee vs IT at $5,025, despite similar project workloads. 
This pay gap may create an IT retention risk over time.

**3. Significant productivity efficiency gap (3× difference)**  
Grace completes 8 projects in 175 hours; David completes 3 in 150 hours. 
High-efficiency employees are not compensated proportionally to their output.

**4. Performance is individual, not departmental**  
40% of employees are rated Excellent, 40% Good, and 20% Average. 
No single department dominates performance ratings.

---

### Recommendations

| Priority | Action | Rationale |
|----------|--------|-----------|
| High | Conduct IT salary audit | IT workload matches Finance but salary lags 22% behind |
| High | Introduce performance-based bonuses | Top performers like Grace and Sarah are undercompensated relative to output |
| Medium | Launch peer knowledge-sharing programme | Pair Average-rated employees with Excellent-rated peers to raise team efficiency |
| Medium | Replace simulated data with real HR records | Enables scalable, automated reporting via SQL + R Markdown |

---

### Limitations

> This analysis is based on a 10-person simulated dataset. Findings are directional only 
> and should be validated against a larger real-world HR dataset before informing 
> policy decisions. Salary figures are assumed to be monthly USD values.
